name: Combined factor V and VIII deficiency (LMAN1/MCFD2)
aliases: combined deficiency of factor V and factor VIII

clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder in which factor V and factor VIII are simultaneously reduced, usually to mild-to-moderate levels around 5 to 30 percent
It is a defect of intracellular protein transport, not of the coagulation factor genes themselves, so both factors are affected together
The bleeding tendency is generally mild to moderate, with mucosal bleeding, easy bruising, and bleeding after surgery, dental work, or childbirth
Both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, reflecting the combined deficiency
It is relatively more frequent in populations with consanguinity, such as those around the Mediterranean and Middle East
It must be distinguished from coincidental co-inheritance of separate factor V and factor VIII deficiencies and from acquired combined deficiencies
Bleeding episodes are managed with sources that replace both factors, using plasma for factor V and factor VIII replacement or antifibrinolytics for mucosal bleeding
reference.pathophysiology: Combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency results from loss-of-function variants in LMAN1 (encoding ERGIC-53) or its cofactor MCFD2. Together these proteins form a cargo receptor that transports factor V and factor VIII from the endoplasmic reticulum through the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment for secretion. When this transport machinery fails, both factors are inefficiently secreted, so their plasma levels fall in parallel despite normal factor V and factor VIII genes. The shared secretory pathway explains why two functionally distinct factors are deficient at once.
additionalDifferentials: Coincidental co-inheritance of separate factor V and factor VIII deficiencies
Acquired combined deficiency from liver disease
Vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect (multiple factor reduction)
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, both prolonged
Specific factor V and factor VIII activity assays confirming concurrent reduction
Von Willebrand factor studies to show factor VIII reduction is not due to von Willebrand disease
Liver function tests to exclude an acquired cause
LMAN1 and MCFD2 gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis
Family studies given the autosomal recessive inheritance and consanguinity
redFlags: Bleeding after major trauma requiring dual-factor replacement
reference.prognosis: The disorder generally causes only mild to moderate bleeding, and with appropriate replacement around surgery and childbirth the long-term outlook is good. Spontaneous severe bleeding is uncommon.
pitfalls: Treating only one factor and leaving the other uncorrected during bleeding
Assuming a low factor VIII reflects von Willebrand disease without checking factor V
Confusing the inherited transport defect with an acquired combined deficiency
Overlooking the diagnosis when both prolonged clotting times are attributed to liver disease
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
